claim: Amazon Verified Permissions (AVP) is a scalable, fine-grained permissions management and authorization service for custom applications; it externalizes authorization from application code, uses the Cedar policy language, and 'presumes that the principal has been previously identified and authenticated through other means' (authN, identity, and data collection are explicitly out of scope).
page_title: What is Amazon Verified Permissions? - Amazon Verified Permissions User Guide
notes: Also documents console/CLI/SDK/CDK access paths and related services (Cognito, API Gateway, IAM Identity Center). States AVP currently uses Cedar version 4.7.

claim: IsAuthorized returns a decision with valid values 'ALLOW | DENY' plus 'determiningPolicies' (the policy IDs that produced the decision) and 'errors' (evaluation errors). Implicit deny returns an empty determiningPolicies list. No third outcome (e.g., review/challenge) exists.
page_title: IsAuthorized - Amazon Verified Permissions API Reference
notes: Supports B04 (binary allow/deny only) and B05 (policy IDs as machine-readable reasons).

claim: IsAuthorized accepts principal, action, resource, a free-form 'context' object, and caller-supplied 'entities' (principals/resources with arbitrary attributes and parent hierarchies) that 'can be referenced and checked by conditional elements in the policies'. Actions must be defined in the schema, not passed as entities.
page_title: IsAuthorized - Amazon Verified Permissions API Reference
notes: Fully caller-defined attribute model; supports arbitrary merchant/customer data evaluation (B06).

claim: BatchIsAuthorized evaluates up to 30 authorization requests per call (entities may contain up to 100 principals and 100 resources); either the principal or the resource must be identical across all requests in a batch; results are returned in request order with per-request decision and determining policies. IAM permission for the batch API is 'verifiedpermissions:IsAuthorized'.
page_title: BatchIsAuthorized - Amazon Verified Permissions API Reference
notes: Also documents that AVP admin/data APIs are governed by AWS IAM action-level permissions (supports G02).

claim: IsAuthorizedWithToken makes authorization decisions from an OIDC JWT (identityToken and/or accessToken); AVP validates token expiration and signature; principal attributes are taken only from the token. Important caveat: 'Tokens from an identity source user continue to be usable until they expire. Token revocation and resource deletion have no effect on the validity of a token in your policy store'.
page_title: IsAuthorizedWithToken - Amazon Verified Permissions API Reference
notes: Principal identity/state lives in the IdP (Cognito/OIDC), not in AVP (supports B07 scoring).

claim: Cedar authorization semantics are deterministic and documented: default deny ('no request is authorized... unless there is a specific permit policy'), 'any satisfied forbid policy overrides' permit, and skip-on-error (a policy that errors is excluded from the decision). The response contains the decision, the determining policies, and diagnostics/errors.
page_title: Authorization - Cedar Policy Language Reference Guide
notes: Well-defined conflict resolution without numeric priorities (supports B08).

claim: Cedar policies are permit/forbid statements with a scope over principal/action/resource using ==, in (hierarchy membership), and is (type test), plus optional 'when {…}' / 'unless {…}' condition clauses that evaluate request context, entity attributes, and relationships. Annotations (e.g., @id("…")) are allowed and 'have no impact on policy evaluation'.
page_title: Basic policy construction in Cedar - Cedar Policy Language Reference Guide
notes: Arbitrary attribute logic (RBAC + ABAC + group hierarchies); annotations could carry metadata such as citations but are inert.

claim: Policy templates contain ?principal / ?resource placeholders; template-linked policies are instantiated from them, and 'Updates to the policy template are reflected across all policies that use the template' (dynamic propagation). Templates can be named and referenced by name.
page_title: Amazon Verified Permissions policy templates and template-linked policies
notes: Reuse mechanism is intra-policy-store; there is no cross-store or marketplace-style policy pack distribution (relevant to J09).

claim: A policy store schema declares entity types, attributes, and actions; schemas are 'optional, but... highly recommended for production'. With policy validation set to Strict, 'all attempts to create or update a policy or policy template are validated against the schema' and invalid policies are rejected.
page_title: Amazon Verified Permissions policy store schema / policy validation mode
notes: Second URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/verifiedpermissions/latest/userguide/policy-validation-mode.html. Type-checked policy authoring (supports G06, B06).

claim: The console test bench simulates authorization requests (Visual and JSON modes) against the policies in a policy store, including context and entity hierarchies, and 'displays the decision to allow or deny the request along with information about the policies satisfied or the errors encountered'.
page_title: Using the Amazon Verified Permissions test bench
notes: Manual pre-deployment simulation tool; no production shadow/dry-run mode and no bulk replay of historical traffic.

claim: Documented service quotas: IsAuthorized and IsAuthorizedWithToken default 200 requests/second per Region per policy store (adjustable); BatchIsAuthorized 30 RPS (adjustable); policy size 10,000 bytes; schema 100,000 bytes; 30,000 policy stores per Region per account; 40 policy templates per store; 1 identity source per store; authorization request size 1 MB; policy size per resource 200,000 bytes; 100 transitive parents per entity.
page_title: Quotas for Amazon Verified Permissions
notes: Fully published rate limits (supports H07); default TPS is modest but adjustable; 30k stores/Region supports per-tenant store architectures (G01).

claim: CloudTrail integration: all management events (CreatePolicy, PutSchema, etc.) are logged automatically; authorization calls are data events — 'Data events like IsAuthorized and IsAuthorizedWithToken are not logged by default when you create a trail'; customers must explicitly enable data-event logging (extra CloudTrail cost). For authorization calls 'the response elements, such as the decision, are included under additionalEventData'.
page_title: Logging Amazon Verified Permissions API calls using AWS CloudTrail
notes: Documented example entries show clientToken idempotency parameters on create APIs, userIdentity (who), eventTime (when), and decision per request. Decision logging exists but is opt-in and customer-assembled.

claim: The documented CloudTrail data-event examples for IsAuthorized/BatchIsAuthorized record principal, action, resource, policyStoreId, and the decision — but NOT the determining policy IDs, the request context, or the entity attributes submitted with the request.
page_title: Logging Amazon Verified Permissions API calls using AWS CloudTrail (log file entries)
notes: Based on the documented example log entries (sample requests contained no context/entities, so context logging is unproven; determining policies are demonstrably absent from additionalEventData). Full evidence-grade reconstruction requires the application to log requests/responses itself.

claim: Public pricing: 'Single Authorization Request $0.000005 per API request' ($5/million); batch authorization tiered at $0.00015 (first 40M/mo), $0.000075 (next 60M), $0.00004 (>100M) where 'Each call to BatchIsAuthorized or BatchIsAuthorizedWithToken API is metered as one request, irrespective of the number of authorizations you make within the API request'; policy management $0.00004 per request; 'There are no upfront or minimum fees'.
page_title: Amazon Verified Permissions Pricing
notes: A 30-decision batch call costs one batch fee, so batching can reach ~$5/million decisions even at tier-1 batch pricing. Worked examples on page: $25/mo for 5M single requests.

claim: On June 12, 2025 AWS reduced the single authorization request price by up to 97%, to $5 per million requests (previously ~$150/million at tier 1); batch and policy-management pricing unchanged.
page_title: Amazon Verified Permissions reduces authorization request price by up to 97%
notes: Signals aggressive commoditization of the managed authorization-decision layer.

claim: Published SLA with service credits: 10% credit for monthly uptime below 99.9%, 25% below 99.0%, 100% below 95.0%; availability is measured per 5-minute interval on the authorization APIs (IsAuthorized, IsAuthorizedWithToken).
page_title: Amazon Verified Permissions Service Level Agreement
notes: Standard AWS-style SLA; the effective commitment threshold is 99.9% monthly uptime.

claim: Amazon Verified Permissions is HIPAA eligible (announced October 14, 2024); customers with an AWS BAA can use it for workloads subject to HIPAA.
page_title: Amazon Verified Permissions is now HIPAA eligible

claim: Amazon Verified Permissions is in scope for AWS SOC 1, 2, and 3 reports (listed on the AWS 'Services in Scope by Compliance Program' SOC page).
page_title: AWS Services in Scope by Compliance Program - SOC

claim: As of August 29, 2025 AVP is available in 35 AWS Regions, including AWS GovCloud (US-East/US-West), and (September 2025) the AWS China (Beijing and Ningxia) Regions.
page_title: Amazon Verified Permissions is available in four additional regions
notes: GovCloud availability corroborated by https://docs.aws.amazon.com/govcloud-us/latest/UserGuide/govcloud-verifiedpermissions.html; China by amazonaws.cn announcement. Regional service — no built-in multi-region policy replication; each policy store lives in one Region.

claim: Named customers: TELUS (smart-home device access), Grosvenor Engineering Group (asset access across 45,000 buildings), Stedi (healthcare clearinghouse; 'By batching authorization requests and caching decisions, we are able to cost-effectively process up to 700M requests per month with low latencies'), Twilio Flex ('centralized control for permissions audits, with distributed decision-making'), FIS (Prophet insurance solution with compliance requirements).
page_title: Fine-Grained Authorization – Amazon Verified Permissions Customers – AWS
notes: Vendor-selected quotes; demonstrates enterprise adoption incl. regulated industries (healthcare EDI, financial services) but shallow public implementation detail.

claim: AWS recommends 'creating one policy store per application, or one policy store per tenant for multi-tenant applications'; namespaces (up to 100 per store) disambiguate tenants; policy store aliases give friendly names; deletion protection is enabled by default for console-created stores.
page_title: Amazon Verified Permissions policy stores
notes: Combined with the 30,000 stores/Region quota, per-tenant isolation is a documented, supported architecture.

claim: AWS Prescriptive Guidance for AVP as a PDP states policy version tracking is the customer's job: 'you should use a continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipeline to administer, modify, and track policy versions... application logic doesn't inherently perform this functionality. To support these capabilities in your application, you must explicitly design your application to implement this functionality.' It also states: 'If it's necessary to provide external data from other sources to reach an authorization decision, this data must be retrieved and provided to Verified Permissions as part of the authorization request. Additional context, entities, and attributes are not retrieved by default with this service.'
page_title: Implementing a PDP by using Amazon Verified Permissions - AWS Prescriptive Guidance
notes: Positive official evidence of absence for native policy version history (C05) and for any data/signal-fetching or vendor orchestration (E10, J06). Also supports per-tenant custom roles and cross-tenant guardrail policies (G01).

claim: UpdatePolicy modifies a static policy in place; only the action and when/unless clauses may change (effect, principal, and resource are immutable); responses carry only createdDate and lastUpdatedDate; the service is 'eventually consistent' (changes take a few seconds to propagate). No policy version history or rollback mechanism exists in the API.
page_title: UpdatePolicy - Amazon Verified Permissions API Reference
notes: In-place mutation without version retention; old policy text is unrecoverable from AVP once updated.

claim: The complete AVP API surface is 34 operations: authorization (IsAuthorized, IsAuthorizedWithToken, BatchIsAuthorized, BatchIsAuthorizedWithToken), CRUD for policies/templates/schema/policy stores/identity sources/aliases, BatchGetPolicy, and tagging. There are no decision-log query, decision-replay, simulation, approval-workflow, policy-versioning, or webhook APIs.
page_title: Actions - Amazon Verified Permissions API Reference
notes: Full enumeration of the API used as positive evidence of absence for several capability squares (B10, C08, G04, J02, J03). API wire version is 2021-12-01.

claim: Infrastructure-as-code support: CloudFormation resource AWS::VerifiedPermissions::PolicyStore (with DeletionProtection, Schema, ValidationSettings, Tags properties) plus policy/template/identity-source resources; Terraform hashicorp/aws resources (aws_verifiedpermissions_policy_store, _schema, _policy) and awscc equivalents; an official L2 CDK construct (cdklabs/cdk-verified-permissions).
page_title: AWS::VerifiedPermissions::PolicyStore - AWS CloudFormation
notes: Terraform: https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/aws/latest/docs/resources/verifiedpermissions_schema; CDK: https://github.com/cdklabs/cdk-verified-permissions. Enables GitOps-style policy deployment pipelines.

claim: Policy store deletion protection (announced April 2025) 'prevents the policy store from being deleted by any user' until explicitly deactivated; enabled by default for console-created stores, disabled by default via API/SDK.
page_title: Amazon Verified Permissions now supports policy store deletion protection
notes: Change-safety control; corroborated in policy-stores.html user guide.

claim: Official SDK support in 10+ languages (.NET, C++, Go, Java, JavaScript, Kotlin, PHP, Python, Ruby, Rust) plus AWS CLI and PowerShell; the API is a stable versioned AWS service API (verifiedpermissions-2021-12-01).
page_title: What is Amazon Verified Permissions? (Accessing Verified Permissions)
notes: SDK-level idempotent create operations use ClientToken parameters (visible in documented CloudTrail request examples).

claim: Packaged integrations: an API Gateway integration in which 'Verified Permissions creates a Lambda authorizer' for REST APIs (authorizer responses cached 120 seconds by default, TTL adjustable); AWS AppSync integration; an Express.js middleware ('protect API endpoints in your Express applications without modifying existing route handlers'); console quick-start wizards that build schemas from an API Gateway API and identity sources from Cognito.
page_title: Control access based on an identity's attributes with Verified Permissions - Amazon API Gateway
notes: Express integration documented in the AVP user guide (integration-express); reduces but does not eliminate integration engineering.

claim: Identity sources connect a policy store to Amazon Cognito user pools or external OIDC identity providers (the FAQ names Okta, Ping Identity, and CyberArk); nonhuman identities (devices, system processes) are supported as principals; quota is 1 identity source per policy store.
page_title: Amazon Verified Permissions FAQs
notes: This is app-user identity for authorization input. Administrative access to AVP itself is via AWS IAM / IAM Identity Center (workforce SSO) as with any AWS service.

claim: Cedar is open source under the Apache-2.0 license, maintained by the cedar-policy GitHub organization (AWS-led): Rust core crates (cedar-policy, cedar-policy-cli, cedar-policy-symcc, cedar-wasm, language server) plus Go (cedar-go) and Java (cedar-java) implementations. 'Cedar is designed for analysis using Automated Reasoning'; policy structure is 'designed to be indexed for quick retrieval and to support fast and scalable real-time evaluation, with bounded latency.'
page_title: cedar-policy/cedar: Implementation of the Cedar Policy Language
notes: Open-source engine means customers can self-host evaluation and use AVP only for management, or leave AVP entirely with policies intact (lowers lock-in).

claim: Cedar was accepted into the CNCF at the Sandbox maturity level on October 8, 2025.
page_title: Cedar - CNCF
notes: Neutral-foundation governance strengthens Cedar's position as an industry-standard policy language beyond AWS.

claim: Cedar was built with 'verification-guided development': an executable formal model in the Lean proof assistant with machine-checked proofs of safety/security properties (e.g., forbid-overrides-permit, sound validation), plus differential random testing of millions of inputs against the production Rust implementation.
page_title: How we built Cedar with automated reasoning and differential testing - Amazon Science
notes: Corroborated by lean-lang.org/use-cases/cedar/ and the cedar-spec repository. A correctness assurance level unusual among rules/policy engines; relevant to regulated-use suitability.

claim: Cedar Analysis (open-sourced June 16, 2025): the Cedar Symbolic Compiler translates policies into SMT formulas (solved with cvc5) and a CLI compares two policy sets as 'Equivalent', 'More Permissive', 'Less Permissive', or 'Incomparable', and detects 'Shadowed Permits', 'Impossible Conditions', 'Forbid Overrides', and 'Complete Denials'; the compiler is implemented in Lean with proofs of soundness and completeness. It is an open-source tool, not an integrated AVP service feature.
page_title: Introducing Cedar Analysis: Open Source Tools for Verifying Authorization Policies - AWS Open Source Blog
notes: Enables pre-rollout logical change-impact analysis ('does the new policy set allow anything the old one did not?') with counterexamples — but as a CLI the customer must operate, with no data/traffic-based impact estimation.

claim: Cedar has datetime and duration extension types (RFC 0080; millisecond precision, comparison operators, .toTime()); temporal conditions depend entirely on the caller supplying the current time in context (e.g., context.now) — the engine has no clock, and 'if the application forgets to include it in the context, datetime conditions silently fail'. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Policy demonstrates the pattern with a system-provided context.system.now, including a documented 'Promotional period policy' example ('Allow refunds only during January 2025') and business-hours windows; 'The Policy Engine does not support timezone conversions' (UTC only).
page_title: Time-based policy support - Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
notes: Cedar datatypes reference: https://docs.cedarpolicy.com/policies/syntax-datatypes.html and RFC https://github.com/cedar-policy/rfcs/blob/main/text/0080-datetime-extension.md. In AVP itself the application must pass time in context; AVP has no scheduled policy activation/expiry (no such API — see AWSCEDAR-024).

claim: Cedar is becoming AWS's cross-product policy language: AWS Verified Access policies are written in Cedar; Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Policy uses Cedar to authorize AI-agent tool calls (with natural-language policy generation); cedar-access-control-for-k8s applies Cedar to Kubernetes authorization/admission; and Dogwood (announced August 6, 2026, Apache-2.0) extends Cedar with 'when temporal { … }' clauses over event history (operators: formerly, count_within, count_distinct_within, sum_within) for sequence-aware rules — 'any syntactically valid Cedar policy is a syntactically valid Dogwood policy'.
page_title: Introducing Dogwood: runtime verification for AI agents - AWS Open Source Blog
notes: Verified Access: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/verified-access/latest/ug/auth-policies.html; AgentCore Cedar: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/why-policy-in-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-chose-cedar-for-securing-agentic-workflows/; K8s: https://github.com/cedar-policy/cedar-access-control-for-k8s. Shows AWS investing in Cedar breadth (incl. temporal/sequence and rate-limit-like rules) — relevant to replacement risk.

claim: Official latency statements: applications can 'evaluate access requests in milliseconds' (Prescriptive Guidance; FAQ says authorization requests are evaluated in 'milliseconds'); Cedar is designed for 'fast, scalable, real-time evaluation with bounded latency'. No specific p50/p99 latency SLOs are published.
page_title: Implementing a PDP by using Amazon Verified Permissions - AWS Prescriptive Guidance
notes: Network round-trip to a regional AWS endpoint applies; Stedi case cites 'low latencies' at 700M req/month using batching and client-side caching.

claim: AVP has no native webhooks or event bus: 'Verified Permissions sends service events to EventBridge via AWS CloudTrail' only (best-effort delivery of API-call events); there are no service-originated notification events.
page_title: Amazon Verified Permissions events - Amazon EventBridge
notes: Change notifications can be assembled from CloudTrail-sourced EventBridge rules (e.g., on CreatePolicy), but this is generic AWS plumbing, not a product webhook feature.

claim: CloudTrail log file integrity validation (inheritable by AVP audit logs): SHA-256 hashing and SHA-256/RSA-signed hourly digest files chained to prior digests make it 'computationally infeasible to modify, delete or forge CloudTrail log files without detection'; validated logs support asserting 'that particular user credentials performed specific API activity'.
page_title: Validating CloudTrail log file integrity - AWS CloudTrail
notes: Platform capability of CloudTrail, not an AVP feature; applies to AVP management and (if enabled) data events. Retention is customer-managed in S3/Glacier.

claim: The AVP monitoring documentation lists exactly one monitoring tool — AWS CloudTrail. No service-specific CloudWatch metrics, dashboards, or decision-analytics tooling are documented for Verified Permissions.
page_title: Monitoring Amazon Verified Permissions API calls
notes: Absence by enumeration of the official monitoring section; customers build observability from CloudTrail (and their own application logs).

claim: The FAQ positions CloudTrail as providing 'an audit trail of policy changes including who made changes and when', supporting compliance tracking of policy administration.
page_title: Amazon Verified Permissions FAQs
notes: Change attribution (who/when) exists; documented CloudTrail examples do not show the policy statement text in the event, so content-diff history requires external tooling (e.g., git/IaC).

claim: Amazon Verified Permissions became generally available on June 13, 2023.
page_title: Amazon Verified Permissions is now generally available
notes: ~3 years in market as of research date.

claim: AVP tracks Cedar language versions as a managed upgrade: the user guide states 'Verified Permissions currently uses Cedar version 4.7' (Cedar 4.5 support was announced August 2025); the service API itself is the stable versioned AWS API verifiedpermissions-2021-12-01.
page_title: What is Amazon Verified Permissions? (Cedar policy language)
notes: Cedar 4.5 announcement: https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/08/amazon-verified-permissions-cedar-4-5

claim: Product positioning: 'fully managed authorization service' implementing Zero Trust-aligned, policy-based access control; stated audiences are developers building applications with granular permissions, security and audit teams, and architects; featured use cases are application permissions (smart home, building assets, healthcare transactions, contact centers, financial services applications) — not marketing, promotions, or regulatory compliance workflows.
page_title: Fine-Grained Authorization - Amazon Verified Permissions - AWS
notes: Buyer is engineering/platform + security; no legal, marketing, or fraud/risk buyer motion.
